paragraphs: Sparse coding learns a compact description of an image using a limited set of active features. The paper addresses a source of redundancy in earlier sparse coding and independent component analysis approaches: a feature can be learned repeatedly because it appears at different image locations. Without explicitly accounting for transformations, the representation can treat these appearances as separate features.

The authors introduce a bilinear generative model that represents interactions between image features and their transformations. This gives the coding algorithm a way to describe both a feature and how it appears in an image. The approach helps reduce repeated representations and provides a basis for vision that can recognize features despite transformations.

The paper demonstrates bilinear sparse coding on natural images and explores an extension that captures spatial relationships among an object's independent features. That extension connects the coding problem to recognition based on object parts. The contribution is both a less redundant image representation and a proposed framework for representing how parts belong together.
neurips-2002-a-bilinear-model-for-sparse.tldr: A bilinear sparse coding model represents features together with their transformations to reduce redundant image codes.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how neural circuits could process an ongoing stream of sensory information while the environment changes rapidly. The input is multimodal, so the problem involves multiple kinds of information arriving continuously. The computational challenge is to explain how recurrent circuits of integrate-and-fire neurons can handle this stream in real time.

The proposed model brings together principles from high-dimensional dynamical systems and statistical learning theory. The dynamical perspective concerns the evolving activity of a recurrent circuit, while the learning perspective connects that activity to computation. Together, these perspectives frame neural processing as something that happens through a circuit's changing state as inputs arrive.

A central feature of the proposal is that it can be implemented on generic recurrent circuitry, including circuitry that has evolved or is otherwise available. This makes the relationship between ordinary recurrent neural organization and real-time computation the main contribution. The abstract presents a computational model for this challenge, rather than an experimental demonstration of particular performance levels.
neurips-2002-a-model-for-real-time-compu.tldr: The paper proposes a model combining dynamical systems and learning theory for real-time computation in generic recurrent neural circuits.

paragraphs: The paper builds a binary classifier from simple decision boundaries defined by pairs of training examples from opposite classes. Each pair supplies a candidate hyperplane, called a dyadic hypercut. Kernel functions satisfying Mercer's conditions extend these simple boundaries to nonlinear classification, allowing the same construction to represent more complex separations.

A confidence-rated version of AdaBoost adds hypercuts incrementally to form an ensemble. Boosting provides a strategy for searching the finite collection of candidate boundaries, and the resulting classifier tends to increase the classification margin. The incremental construction also gives direct control over the number of kernel evaluations, allowing prediction cost to be traded against accuracy.

On the reported UCI datasets, generalization was comparable to support vector machines and nearest-neighbor classifiers. Prediction cost was similar to or better than that of support vector machines. These findings support the method as an online, incremental alternative with an adjustable computational budget; they do not establish that it is uniformly more accurate or faster.
neurips-2002-boosted-dyadic-kernel-discr.tldr: Boosting simple boundaries defined by opposite-class example pairs produces incremental kernel classifiers with controllable prediction cost.

paragraphs: The paper asks what determines the thickness of axon branches. Its starting hypothesis is that axonal dimensions have evolved to balance two demands: transmitting signals with little delay and keeping the total volume of the branching structure small. The question becomes whether this tradeoff predicts a relationship between the thicknesses of connected branches.

The authors derive a branching law for optimal diameters under a general cost function. At a split, the parent diameter raised to the power v + 2 equals the sum of the two daughter diameters raised to that same power. Here, v describes the assumed relationship between axon diameter and signal conduction speed. The predicted geometry therefore depends on how diameter affects propagation.

The authors compare the law with available experimental measurements and report reasonable agreement. That agreement supports the proposed optimization account without establishing that the tradeoff is the sole determinant of axonal shape. The contribution is a quantitative connection between a functional hypothesis about neural wiring and the geometry of individual branch points.
neurips-2002-branching-law-for-axons-89a.tldr: Balancing signal delay against axon volume yields a branching law that agrees reasonably with available measurements.

paragraphs: The paper examines how people learn categories from examples, with particular attention to categories that differ in complexity. It proposes an account based on minimum description length: the complexity of a concept is expressed through the length of its description. This provides a common way to discuss both simple, regular categories and highly irregular ones.

The authors test a broad range of two-dimensional concept structures. Including irregular categories matters because the supplied account notes that earlier theories had often been tested on a narrower collection of simple categories. A theory that explains only these simpler cases has faced a different challenge from one evaluated across a wider range of structures.

The minimum description length account fits participants' performance well across the tested concepts. The authors interpret this as evidence that a concept's intrinsic description length systematically influences how learnable it is. The result supports complexity as an organizing principle for human category learning, while remaining an empirical account of performance on the category types studied.
neurips-2002-categorization-under-comple.tldr: Human learning of simple and complex categories is well explained by an account based on minimum description length.

paragraphs: Bayesian mixture methods predict by taking a weighted average of candidate functions. Such methods can be optimal in several settings when the prior information is sufficiently accurate. This paper asks what can still be guaranteed when some prior assumptions are wrong, a situation in which those familiar optimality results do not directly settle performance.

The authors establish bounds that depend on the observed data and apply to a finite training sample. Their analysis extends earlier work on randomized methods, including the Gibbs algorithm, to fully Bayesian mixtures. The focus is therefore on guarantees for the mixture predictor itself, beyond the earlier randomized setting.

These guarantees support using Bayesian mixtures in agnostic settings where the usual Bayesian assumptions fail to hold. They provide a way to assess such procedures without requiring all of those assumptions to be correct. The derived bounds also apply directly to non-Bayesian mixture methods, including bagging and boosting, giving the analysis relevance beyond Bayesian prediction.
neurips-2002-data-dependent-bounds-for-b.tldr: Data-dependent finite-sample bounds give Bayesian mixture predictors guarantees even when usual Bayesian assumptions fail.

paragraphs: Learning a nonlinear dynamic system can involve information about both its outputs and how those outputs change locally. The paper uses Gaussian processes to combine ordinary function observations with derivative observations in one empirical model. It also incorporates uncertainty associated with the derivative information, so these observations need not be treated as exact.

Derivative information can come from expert-specified priors or from perturbation experiments near equilibrium. The framework can also combine multiple local linear models consistently. Its integrability constraints ensure that the local derivative descriptions fit together as parts of a consistent function model, making the fusion more than a collection of unrelated local approximations.

The approach also addresses the computational burden of training Gaussian process models. Large amounts of near-equilibrium data can be summarized by a small number of linearizations, reducing the training set size. The authors report a dramatic efficiency improvement for dynamic system identification through this compression, connecting local system knowledge to both coherent inference and more manageable computation.
neurips-2002-derivative-observations-in-.tldr: Gaussian processes combine uncertain derivative information and ordinary observations to model dynamic systems consistently and more efficiently.

paragraphs: Classification trees are attractive because they are relatively easy to implement and interpret, but their widespread use has not been matched by equally extensive performance theory. This paper introduces dyadic classification trees and analyzes them using structural risk minimization. That theoretical framework also supplies the rule used to prune the trees.

The authors show that these trees are nearly optimal in a minimax sense across a broad range of classification problems. This concerns performance relative to the best achievable worst-case behavior within the relevant problem classes. Consequently, in many of these cases, other methods cannot improve substantially on their performance; it is not a claim of superiority on every dataset.

The paper also shows that this statistical performance is attainable with growing and pruning algorithms whose complexity is linear in the number of training examples. On benchmark datasets, the trees compare favorably with standard CART. The contribution joins broad theoretical guarantees with computational efficiency and favorable empirical results in one tree-learning framework.
neurips-2002-dyadic-classification-trees.tldr: Dyadic classification trees achieve broad minimax near-optimality guarantees with growing and pruning costs linear in training-set size.

paragraphs: The paper examines how people's causal judgments develop during learning. Its motivation is that existing psychological theories primarily emphasize long-run predictions. Explaining judgments after learning has progressed is a different task from explaining the short-run behavior that occurs as a person is still learning about causal relationships.

The authors consider three theories of causal learning and judgment. Two describe learning through the estimation of parameters in causal Bayesian networks, using different parameterizations. The third describes learning through changes in structure. These alternatives distinguish learning about the numerical properties of a causal model from learning about the organization of the model itself.

The paper develops dynamical versions of these theories and compares their predictions with a real-world dataset. The contribution is to bring their accounts of the learning process into direct comparison, rather than considering only their long-run predictions. This makes the evolution of causal judgments the object of explanation and provides a way to examine how different theories describe short-run human behavior.
neurips-2002-dynamical-causal-learning-d.tldr: The paper compares dynamical versions of three causal-learning theories to study people's short-run judgments.

paragraphs: Sensory environments contain both ongoing noise and changes that challenge an existing interpretation. The paper argues that these forms of variability can have different computational, behavioral, and neural roles. It develops a theoretical distinction between expected and unexpected uncertainty and connects that distinction to two neuromodulatory systems.

The authors refine their account of acetylcholine in cortical inference using expected uncertainty. They also propose that norepinephrine signals unexpected uncertainty, specifically a major disagreement between incoming sensory information and the brain's prevailing interpretation. In this account, the mismatch signal influences both current inference and plasticity, linking interpretation of inputs with changes in what is learned.

An adaptive factor analysis model illustrates the proposal. Its role is to make the computational account concrete, showing how the distinction can be expressed in a model that adapts. The paper presents a theory of differentiated neuromodulatory roles, supported by this illustration, rather than establishing that either chemical has only one function or that the proposed biological assignment is certain.
neurips-2002-expected-and-unexpected-unc.tldr: The paper proposes distinct roles for acetylcholine and norepinephrine in signaling expected and unexpected uncertainty.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a generative model for the tree structures used in natural language parsing. It assigns separate scores to lexical dependency structure and syntactic structure. The former supplies the model's semantic component, while a probabilistic context-free grammar supplies its syntactic component. The complete model brings these separately scored aspects together.

This factorization makes the modeling choices easier to separate conceptually. It also gives researchers straightforward opportunities to improve either component on its own. The authors report performance comparable to similar models that do not use this separation, suggesting that the simpler organization can preserve competitive parsing performance.

The main computational benefit is that the factored model supports a highly effective A* parsing algorithm. This enables efficient, exact inference: the search can identify an optimal parse under the model. Exactness refers to solving the model's inference problem, while parsing performance concerns how well its predictions match the task. The paper's contribution connects a modular model design with an efficient way to solve that model.
neurips-2002-fast-exact-inference-with-a.tldr: Separately scoring lexical dependencies and syntax enables efficient exact A* parsing with performance comparable to similar non-factored models.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the computational cost of comparing discrete structures such as strings and trees. These objects require matching procedures suited to their structure. The authors introduce an algorithm that performs this matching in linear time, replacing the quadratic-time dynamic programming approach discussed in the abstract.

This matters because the cost of matching can make kernel methods difficult to use on structured objects. Linear growth means that the matching work scales proportionally with the relevant input size, whereas quadratic growth increases much faster. The contribution therefore changes the computational scaling of the matching operation, rather than merely claiming a small implementation speedup.

The authors also show that prediction can, in many cases, have cost linear in the length of the sequence being classified, independent of the number of support vectors. That qualification is part of the claim: the abstract does not assert it for every case. Together, faster matching and the conditional prediction improvement make string kernels a more practical option for applications.
neurips-2002-fast-kernels-for-string-and.tldr: A linear-time matching algorithm makes structured kernels cheaper, with prediction cost independent of support-vector count in many cases.

paragraphs: The paper studies classification when data arrive as a matrix of relationships between row objects and column objects. These objects may come from different sets. The authors interpret each entry as the output of an unknown kernel and show that, under mild assumptions, these kernels correspond to dot products in an unknown feature space.

They derive a model-selection objective by minimizing a generalization-error bound based on covering numbers. This follows structural risk minimization and permits matrices that are not positive definite, symmetric, or even square. When rows represent features, an additional sparsity constraint turns the same framework into a feature-selection method.

The authors apply the method to DNA microarray data, with genes as rows, samples as columns, and expression levels as entries. Their method selects a sparse set of genes and achieves superior classification results in the reported benchmarks. Those comparisons include single-gene classification and support vector machines and nearest neighbors following standard feature selection. The findings connect the general matrix framework to compact feature sets in this application.
neurips-2002-feature-selection-and-class.tldr: A generalization-bound objective supports classification on general relationship matrices and sparse gene selection with strong reported benchmark results.

paragraphs: Nonlinear dimensionality reduction seeks a lower-dimensional representation of data whose structure need not be captured by a linear transformation. The paper organizes existing approaches into two broad groups: global methods, represented by Isomap, and local methods, represented by Locally Linear Embedding and Laplacian Eigenmaps. Each group offers different advantages and disadvantages.

The authors present two variants of Isomap intended to combine benefits from these groups. They retain advantages of the global approach while incorporating computational sparsity and the ability to invert conformal maps. These are the two properties that the abstract identifies as previously exclusive advantages of local methods.

The importance of the result is that choosing a global approach need not exclude those particular local-method benefits. Computational sparsity concerns how much of the relevant computation must be represented or carried out, while conformal-map inversion concerns the kinds of mappings the method can handle. The contribution is a pair of algorithmic variants that narrow this specific divide between global and local dimensionality reduction.
neurips-2002-global-versus-local-methods.tldr: Two Isomap variants combine global-method advantages with computational sparsity and the ability to invert conformal maps.

paragraphs: The paper develops independent component analysis for high-dimensional datasets containing missing entries. Rather than requiring a complete dataset before estimating independent sources, the method handles unobserved entries within a Bayesian generative model. Integrating that model allows learning to proceed using the information that is actually observed.

Each independent source has a distribution modeled by a mixture of Gaussians. This flexibility allows the sources to differ in skewness and kurtosis, capturing different distribution shapes. Variational Bayesian learning also automatically determines the data's dimensionality. The authors describe the resulting density model as accurate for the observed data and free of overfitting problems.

The learned density supports direct probability estimation for missing values in the original high-dimensional space. That is useful because the output can describe uncertainty about an absent entry rather than only supplying a replacement value. The approach also avoids a separate dimensionality-reduction preprocessing step, which the abstract identifies as infeasible with missing data. Missing-value inference and representation learning are thus handled within the same framework.
neurips-2002-handling-missing-data-with-.tldr: Variational Bayesian ICA learns flexible source distributions from incomplete high-dimensional data and estimates probabilities for missing values.

paragraphs: The paper introduces kernels that use the geometry of statistical models to define similarity for learning. Its starting point is the Fisher information metric, which gives the space of statistical models a geometric structure. The authors then use the heat equation on that space to construct a family of information diffusion kernels.

These kernels generalize the Gaussian kernel from ordinary Euclidean space to the geometry associated with statistical models. This creates a connection between generative modeling and nonparametric discriminative learning: a statistical model supplies the structure from which a learning kernel is built. A special case provides a new way to apply kernel algorithms to discrete data.

The paper contributes both theoretical analysis and an application. Using spectral theory from differential geometry, the authors prove bounds on covering numbers for the kernels, addressing their mathematical complexity. They also present text-classification experiments. Together, these contributions develop the construction, analyze its properties, and illustrate its use on discrete observations without asserting a particular comparative improvement in the abstract.
neurips-2002-information-diffusion-kerne.tldr: Information diffusion kernels use statistical-model geometry to connect generative modeling with kernel-based discriminative learning.

paragraphs: The paper develops algorithms for learning the structure of graphical models from data. A central challenge is handling variables of different kinds within one framework. The proposed approach supports hybrid graphs containing discrete and continuous variables, allowing the structure-learning procedure to work with both rather than requiring a single variable type.

The algorithms use kernel generalized variance, a measure built from Mercer kernels. The construction effectively treats variables as Gaussians in a kernel-induced feature space, putting different variable types on a common footing. This Gaussian treatment belongs to the feature-space representation; the framework accommodates original variables of arbitrary type.

The authors also examine the computational properties of this construction. They show how the kernel trick permits the relevant statistics to be computed in linear time, making the common representation computationally useful. Experiments involving discrete and continuous data illustrate the framework. The stated efficiency result concerns computation of those statistics, rather than an unrestricted claim that every part of graphical-model structure search takes linear time.
neurips-2002-learning-graphical-models-w.tldr: Kernel generalized variance provides a common framework for learning graphical models with mixed discrete and continuous variables.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a statistical framework for deriving learning rules in networks of spiking neurons. The starting point is to specify both the neurons' dynamics and the function the network should perform. From those choices, the framework derives optimal local learning rules, tying their optimality to the particular model and task.

The authors apply this approach to learning temporal sequences. They derive local rules for a spiking-neuron model and demonstrate better performance than correlation-based Hebbian approaches. The significance is methodological as well as empirical: the learning rule follows from the stated dynamics and desired function, providing a principled alternative to assuming a rule in advance.

The framework can incorporate synaptic depression, and the authors outline how it could extend to networks with more complex spiking neurons. They also consider stochastic release of discrete vesicles and discuss what this implies for learning complexity. These additions connect the statistical derivation to richer neural mechanisms while keeping the relationship between neuronal dynamics and learning central.
neurips-2002-learning-in-spiking-neural-.tldr: A statistical framework derives local learning rules from spiking-neuron dynamics and demonstrates improved temporal-sequence learning over Hebbian approaches.

paragraphs: The paper studies training data in which each example has several candidate class labels, but exactly one is correct. The candidates may be supplied as a set or as a probability distribution. This is a problem of ambiguity in supervision: the learner must resolve which candidate applies while learning how to classify examples.

The authors propose a discriminative approach designed to handle that ambiguity. The setting can arise when words are associated with an image or when labels have a hierarchical organization. These examples motivate learning from partially informative labels, where the supplied candidates constrain the answer without directly identifying it.

Experiments on five UCI datasets show that the method can identify the correct label among the candidates and achieve performance close to training with a single correct label per example. In contrast, the naive methods examined deteriorate rapidly as label ambiguity increases. These findings support the value of modeling the ambiguity explicitly, under the paper's assumption that one candidate is the correct class.
neurips-2002-learning-with-multiple-labe.tldr: A discriminative method learns from ambiguous candidate labels and approaches fully labeled performance on five reported datasets.

paragraphs: The paper examines a modeling question about the temporary difficulty forming new memories associated with midazolam. Does the effect reflect storing less information, or storing information less accurately? These possibilities describe different changes to episodic memory, even though both could impair later recognition.

The authors fit a simple variant of the Bayesian REM model to previously collected recognition-memory data. The data include the effects of midazolam, study time, and normative word frequency, with both yes-no judgments and remember-know judgments. Modeling these observations together allows the proposed account to address several aspects of recognition behavior.

A simple strength model fits the data well, contrary to the expectations described in the abstract. More centrally, within the REM modeling framework, the data are consistent with reduced accuracy of information storage rather than reduced quantity. This is a conclusion about the interpretation supported by that framework and dataset. It gives a specific computational account of the memory impairment without establishing the proposed storage mechanism as a direct biological finding.
neurips-2002-modeling-midazolam-s-effect.tldr: Within a REM memory model, recognition data are consistent with midazolam reducing storage accuracy rather than the amount stored.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Morton-style factorial coding as a way to understand how neural representations integrate information. Its goal is for two or more external aspects of the world to become independent when conditioned on an internal representation. This differs from the objective of methods such as ICA, which seek independent codes themselves.

The authors emphasize that this organization may be invisible in average neural responses. Analyses of mean tuning curves can therefore miss factorial mechanisms that become apparent in spike-count histograms. The methodological point is that the distribution of responses can reveal structure that a summary of their average does not retain.

The paper presents evidence suggesting that the organization of classical and non-classical receptive fields encourages the development of Morton-style codes. It connects this proposal to an earlier account in which stimulus and context have separable effects on perception. The authors suggest that the framework may help explain perceptual organization and inspire unsupervised learning algorithms, while presenting those implications as possibilities.
neurips-2002-morton-style-factorial-codi.tldr: Morton-style coding seeks conditional independence of external factors and may be revealed by spike-count distributions that average responses obscure.

paragraphs: The paper considers detecting unusual or novel cases when there is little knowledge about anything outside a typical class. In this setting, learning focuses on describing the domain of normal examples. The authors motivate the problem through applications such as fault detection, machine diagnostics, and illness identification.

They propose a one-class classifier whose representation uses dissimilarities between objects. Describing an object through its proximity to known examples provides a natural basis for specifying the typical class. Linear programming finds an efficient description based on a small collection of prototype objects, making those prototypes central to the learned representation.

The method offers two further adjustments. Transforming dissimilarities can improve robustness, while reducing the representation set can lower computation cost. These changes address different practical properties of the classifier: sensitivity to the dissimilarity representation and the expense of evaluating it. The paper also compares the approach with a related one-class classifier, though the abstract does not state a direction of advantage for that comparison.
neurips-2002-one-class-lp-classifiers-fo.tldr: Linear programming learns a compact, prototype-based description of typical objects using dissimilarities for one-class classification.

paragraphs: The paper adapts the large-margin principle to ranking, where the ordering of classes matters. Instead of treating classes only as unrelated alternatives, the proposed methods use margins between neighboring ordered classes. The central design question is how those separations should be allocated and optimized.

The first method uses a fixed-margin policy, maximizing the margin of the closest neighboring classes. The authors describe it as a direct extension of support vector machines to ranking. The second permits a separate margin for each neighboring pair and maximizes their sum. These objectives emphasize different aspects of separation: the tightest neighboring distinction versus the total separation across the ordered classes.

Experiments cover visual classification and collaborative filtering. In the reported comparisons, both approaches outperform existing ordinal-regression algorithms used for ranking and multiclass support vector machines used for general classification. The results support large-margin formulations that explicitly account for order in these tasks. Their significance is empirical: the abstract reports success in those experiments rather than an unconditional performance advantage.
neurips-2002-ranking-with-large-margin-p.tldr: Two large-margin ranking methods optimize either the tightest neighboring-class margin or the sum of distinct neighboring margins.

paragraphs: Greedy importance sampling is an estimation method that searches explicitly for modes in the estimation objective. This search reduces variance relative to standard importance sampling while preserving unbiasedness. The paper builds on earlier work that established feasibility and unbiasedness in both discrete and continuous domains.

The authors reformulate the estimator to remove the free parameters in its original version. They also introduce regularization that further reduces variance without sacrificing unbiasedness. These are distinct benefits: eliminating free parameters simplifies the estimator's specification, while variance reduction makes its estimates less variable without changing their expected target.

The resulting method is shown to work effectively on difficult estimation problems in Markov random field inference. In particular, the authors report improvements over standard Markov chain Monte Carlo estimators when distributions contain multiple sharply peaked modes. That setting is central to the stated finding because the method explicitly searches for modes. The contribution combines a simpler formulation with a regularization strategy that retains the estimator's unbiased character.
neurips-2002-regularized-greedy-importan.tldr: A reformulated greedy importance sampler removes free parameters and reduces variance through regularization while preserving unbiasedness.

paragraphs: Stochastic Neighbor Embedding places objects in a low-dimensional space while trying to preserve who their neighbors are. It accepts either high-dimensional vectors or pairwise dissimilarities. Each object's neighborhood is expressed as a probability distribution, using Gaussian densities for vector inputs or the supplied dissimilarities.

The method constructs corresponding neighbor probabilities in the lower-dimensional representation and tries to make them match the original distributions. Its objective sums a Kullback-Leibler divergence for each object, yielding a simple gradient for adjusting the embedded positions. The representation is therefore optimized around probabilistic neighborhood agreement.

The same framework allows an object to have several widely separated representations. This is useful for ambiguous objects: a word such as bank can appear near both river-related and finance-related concepts. Those separate representations need not pull the two surrounding groups together. The contribution thus includes both a probabilistic neighborhood-preserving embedding and a way to express ambiguity without requiring one location to serve every meaning.
neurips-2002-stochastic-neighbor-embeddi.tldr: Stochastic Neighbor Embedding preserves probabilistic neighborhoods and allows ambiguous objects to occupy multiple low-dimensional locations.
